newsitem.title: UK: Softs Outlook - Sugar to expire, cocoa seen nervous.
newsitem.headline: Softs Outlook - Sugar to expire, cocoa seen nervous.

text.p: LIFFE white sugar futures' May expiry on Tuesday will take the spotlight this week, while cocoa futures will try to overcome nervousness from last week's rollercoaster activity, traders said.
Coffee futures were seen easing amid roasters' absence as they assessed stocks before the March-end financial period.
White sugar's expiry was expected to result in a physical delivery of about two cargoes of European Union origin.
Slack EU sugar demand was seen limiting physical delivery and chances of a short squeeze in London, traders said.

"I think the whites are going through a bit of a slump...at the moment as you're not really shifting sugar, I think people are only taking off the bits and pieces of business that goes on every day," one trader said.
"Nobody is willing to take a big gamble. Everyone is a bit lethargic. I don't think the whites are going to have any real surprises," he said.

Nevertheless, traders would stay watchful of New York because trade houses there were said to be very short in the nearby months, and uncertainty lingered over availability of origins for the May expiry.
After expiry, traders expected the usual cross and against actuals activity as May positions were rolled into August, although one major trade house had been buying May outright.
In cocoa, traders said last week's volatile activity had clouded the near-term outlook and widened July's trading band to between 980 and 1,065 stg per tonne.
Cocoa recovered well from last Monday's tumble to about one-month lows on aggressive fund sales, but technical analysts were not yet ruling out another setback.

Lawrence Eagles, commodity analyst with GNI Ltd, said cocoa's upside path would not be cleared until July hurdled its April 2 peak of 1,065 stg. Before that, July would have to break resistance at 1,034 and minor resistances at 1,049 and 1,062.
But he said sustainable gains could be difficult because of signs this year's cocoa deficit would be smaller than forecasts six months ago due to a larger-than-expected Ivorian crop.

And although fund selling dried up late last week, which allowed cocoa to rise to a weekly high on Friday afternoon, Eagles speculated that funds remained net long the market and could re-emerge to threaten cocoa gains if trade demand did not surface to soak up sales.
Initial July support rested at 985, with critical support at 980. A close below 987 could mean a drop to 940.
Coffee futures were expected to drift lower without any roaster buying activity as roasters returning from Easter continued to assess stocks for the financial period ending March 31.
Origins were also expected to step up selling into any May advance up to $1,700, making further gains to last month's peak of just above $1,800 seem unlikely in the near term.
In robustas, producer sales from Vietnam had eased due to the end of the main crop, and the market was now bracing for sales of the main Indonesian harvest.
"Origins have been quiet. However, scale-up selling is hovering over the market up to $1,700," a trader said.
Indonesia, which was harvesting and shipping its main crop, had been surprisingly quiet, possibly awaiting higher prices.
Immediately, traders said May could drift down to $1,560-$1,540 per tonne this week.
Robusta's fortunes also hinged on sharp swings in New York arabica futures. Traders said a July break below 170 cents per lb could accelerate a fall to the 160-165 area.
A possible Colombia truck strike on April 20 might provide some support, but traders doubted that it would materialise as the government might try to intervene.
